w: Rem Koolhaas dropped an angular white concrete shape onto Boavista's old tram terminus to mark Porto's year as European Capital of Culture. Opened in 2005, it was Portugal's first building designed purely for music, and its faceted, off-kilter shell still looks like nothing else in the city.
s: Portugal's first building built purely for music
_facts: Designed by Rem Koolhaas (OMA), opened 15 April 2005
Built to mark Porto's year as European Capital of Culture (2001)
First building in Portugal conceived exclusively for music, for both performance and training
Built on the site of the old tram terminus at Rotunda da Boavista

w: Attributed to Gustave Eiffel and completed in 1877, this wrought-iron crescent arch leaps 60 metres above the Douro on a single 353-metre span - the longest of its kind anywhere when it opened. Retired from rail duty in 1991, it's often confused with its two-decked neighbour downstream, the Dom Luis Bridge.
s: Eiffel's crescent of iron over the Douro
_facts: Railway bridge built 1877, attributed to Gustave Eiffel
Double-hinged crescent arch, wrought iron, spans 353m, 60m over the Douro River
Was the longest single-arch span in the world at the time of construction
No longer used for rail; replaced by Ponte de Sao Joao in 1991; often confused with the Dom Luis I Bridge

w: This former monastery is built on circles - a round church, a round cloister - a rare geometry that sets it apart from Portugal's usual baroque sprawl. Perched on an outcrop over the Douro, it looks straight down on the Dom Luis I Bridge and Porto's old town, and shares UNESCO World Heritage status with both.
s: A monastery built almost entirely out of circles
_facts: Former monastery in Vila Nova de Gaia, overlooking the Douro opposite Porto
Notable for a circular church and circular cloister
Designated UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 together with the Dom Luis I Bridge and Porto's historic centre

w: Founded in 1997, Portugal's national photography centre opened its first exhibitions that same December on the building's ground floor, running until 2000. A renovation closed it briefly, and it reopened in 2001 - a low-key specialist stop for anyone chasing the country's photographic archive rather than its postcards.
s: Portugal's quiet archive of the photographic image
_facts: Founded in 1997; first exhibitions began December 1997 on the ground floor, running until 2000
Building temporarily closed for renovation, reopened in 2001

n: Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
w: A Modernist Catholic shrine in the parish of Ermesinde, dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and known locally by several names, including the Church of the Good Shepherd. One of greater Porto's newer faces of faith, a plain modern counterpoint to the city's baroque churches downtown.
s: A Modernist shrine with more than one name
_facts: Modernist church in the civil parish of Ermesinde, municipality of Valongo, Porto district
Also known as Church of the Good Shepherd / Sanctuary of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
Catholic shrine dedicated to the worship of the Sacred Heart of Jesus

w: A 14th-century manor house on Rua das Virtudes carries an English club's name - and that's about all the record says, no explanation attached. It sits in the Cedofeita quarter, one of Porto's smaller architectural puzzles, its story quieter than its name suggests.
s: A 14th-century manor with an unexplained English name
_facts: Building on Rua das Virtudes referred to as the English Club of Porto
Located in the civil parish of Cedofeita, Santo Ildefonso, Se, Miragaia, Sao Nicolau e Vitoria, municipality of Porto
